newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Air Afrique says debt crisis over by November.
newsitem.headline: Air Afrique says debt crisis over by November.

text.p: Multinational airline Air Afrique will soon put its debt problems behind it, and can then start generating profits again to prepare for privatisation by 2002, its recently-appointed chief executive said.

Managing director Sir Harry Tirvengadum told Reuters that an agreement on setting up a plane leasing company had been reached in Paris last month at a meeting between Air Afrique, its creditors and ASECNA, a francophone African air safety agency.

"By October 31, everything should be in operation, including the discharging of a part of the debt arrears, and the takeover of four A310-300 planes by the new leasing company, and then their leaseback," he said in an interview.

ASECNA is putting 20 billion CFA francs ($31 million) into the new leasing company, which will also take over the debt contracted to buy the four Airbus planes. Air Afrique's 11 state shareholders have agreed to contribute one billion each.
The debts to be assumed by the leasing company total 117 billion CFA francs.

The four planes are at the heart of Air Afrique's problems. It borrowed in dollars to buy them, but most of its revenue is in CFA francs -- the currency of 10 of its member states -- and, disastrously, the CFA franc was devalued by 50 percent in 1994.
Its total debt today stands at 185 billion CFA francs, with debt for planes accounting for 135 billion, Tirvengadum said.

He took over in February after his predecessor was squeezed out by the member states -- Benin, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Ivory Coast, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Senegal and Togo -- who own about 70 percent of Air Afrique.
Tirvengadum has just completed a cost review and revised the previous management's budget for 1997.
"Unfortunately, it's only for six months of the year, but even so I have managed to reduce the planned deficit from 13.1 billion CFA francs to a little under two billion," he said.
However, that forecast will have to be revised in the light of recent events in Africa, particularly the political conflict in Brazzaville, Congo, that has left hundreds dead.
Air Afrique property there has been looted and cars stolen.
But, mindful of its public service role, Air Afrique has continued to fly to Congo's economic centre of Pointe-Noire, and tried to provide light aircraft to Brazzaville from there.
Similarly, it has been the only airline to guarantee flights to Bangui, capital of the Central African Republic, which has been battered by army mutinies, the latest in June.
"But for Air Afrique, these states would be completely isolated," Tirvengadum said.
An Air Afrique plane crashed on take-off at Douala airport, Cameroon, on Sunday. The plane is a writeoff, Tirvengadum said, but it was only leased by Air Afrique, and fully insured.
Tirvengadum's aim is to have Air Afrique back in the black by 2000, and ready for privatisation by 2002 -- something the member states want, since they can no longer afford subsidies.

It is concentrating on its core activities, and has cut back some flights, but no destinations will be abandoned. In fact, Tirvengadum said he was studying new markets, mentioning in particular Nairobi and the Maghreb countries of North Africa.
But pulling Air Afrique out of the red came first.

"The priority of priorities is to get this company back to profitability..., to make it a little bit more like a commercial company, and a bit less like a public and social service." ($ = 635 CFA francs)
